Pancreastatin inhibitor activates AMPK pathway via GRP78 and ameliorates
dexamethasone induced fatty liver disease in C57BL/6 mice

A B S T R A C T
Aims: To investigate the role of pancreastatin inhibitor (PSTi8) in lipid homeostasis and insulin sensitivity in
dexamethasone induced fatty liver disease associated type 2 diabetes.
Main methods: Glucose releases assay, lipid O staining and ATP/AMP ratio were performed in HepG2 cells.
Twenty four mice were randomly divided into 4 groups: Control group (saline), DEX (1 mg/kg, im) for 17 days,
DEX+PSTi8 (acute 5 mg/kg and chronic 2 mg/kg, ip) for 10 days. The glucose, insulin and pyruvate tolerance
tests (GTT, ITT and PTT), biochemical parameters and Oxymax-CLAMS were performed. Further to elucidate the
action mechanisms of PSTi8, we performed genes expression and western blotting of biological samples.
Key ﬁndings: We found that PSTi8 suppresses hepatic glucose release, lipid deposition, oxidative stress induced
by DEX, stimulates the cellular energy level in hepatocytes and enhances GRP78 activity. It reduces lipogensis
and enhances fatty acid oxidation to improve insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance in DEX induced diabetic
mice. The above cellular eﬀects are the result of activated AMPK signalling pathway in liver, which increases
Srebp1c and ACC phosphorylation. The increased ACC phosphorylation suppresses protein kinase C activity and
enhances insulin sensitivity. The increased expression of UCP3 in liver elicits fatty acid oxidation and energy
expenditure, which suppress oxidative stress.
Signiﬁcance: Thus the activation of AMPK signalling through GRP78, improves lipid homeostasis, enhances
insulin sensitivity via inhibition of PKC activity. PSTi8 suppresses inﬂammation associated with incomplete fatty
acid oxidation. Hence, PSTi8 may be a potential therapeutic agent to treat glucocorticoid-induced fatty liver
associated type 2 diabetes.

immunosuppressive action [2]. Hence it has been used for decades, for
the treatment of numerous inﬂammatory conditions. But on long term
administration DEX induces adverse eﬀects such as, adiposity [3], he-
patic fat deposition [4] and dyslipidaemia [5]. All these characterstics
of metabolic syndrome caused by DEX are positively correlated with the
development of NAFLD [6]. There are several independent factors also,
such as increased free fatty acid uptake [7,8], de-novo lipogenesis [9],
decreased fatty acid oxidation, and reduced very low-density lipopro-
tein (VLDL) secretion, which contributes to hepatic fat accumulation on
GC treatment [10]. There are also evidences that suggests lipid accu-
mulation in the liver is directly responsible for the subsequent devel-
opment of hepatic IR (Mardinoglu et al., 2017) and increased en-
dogenous glucose production, the key elements in the pathogenesis of
type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [11]. The action mechanism of DEX is
via binding to GC receptor and stimulating gluconeogenesis that lead to
hyperglycaemia [12] which lead to inhibition of AMP-activated protein
kinase (AMPK) activity [13], fatty liver diseases [14,15] and insulin
resistance. It was previously reported that the activity of GC receptor
was regulated by AMPK, and it was found that activated AMPK inhibits
GC receptor activity in DEX stimulated condition [16]. So positive
regulation of AMPK activity may be therapeutic target to inhibit DEX
eﬀects.
Previously, our research group reported that pancreastain inhibitor
(PSTi8) interact with glucose response protein 78 (GRP78) and stimu-
lates its activity by competing with pancreastatin (PST) [17]. It was also
found that GRP78 stimulates AMPK activity and knockdown of GRP78
inhibits AMPK signaling [18,19]. Beside this liver speciﬁc loss of GRP78
stimulates lipids accumulation in liver and also get sensitized to a
variety of acute and chronic hepatic disorders by alcohol, a high‐fat
diet, drugs, and toxins [20]. GRP78 inhibition leads to decreases in the
inactivated phosphorylation of acyl coenzyme carboxylases (ACC
Ser79), and ACC is incativated when phosphorylated on Ser79 by AMPK
[21]. Hence GRP78, stimulates phosphorylation of ACC Ser79 by acti-
vating AMPK and improves lipid homeostasis. Furthermore inhibition
of GRP78-ATPase activity and its expression increases glucose 6 phos-
phatase (G6pase) expression which further stimulate hepatic glucose
output [22,23]. So, targeting GRP78 activation may be a therapeutic
target to control DEX induced fatty liver diseases associated type 2
diabetes through AMPK pathway.
So in this study, we hypothesised that PSTi8 may stimulates AMPK
activity by GRP78 and inhibits fatty acid synthesis, elicit its oxidation to
improve lipid homeostasis. The decreased fat accumulation may en-
hance insulin sensitivity and improves glucose homeostasis in DEX-in-
duced fatty liver disease associated with T2DM mice.

2.2. Cell culture
HepG2 (hepatocellular carcinoma cell line) was purchased from the

2.3. Hepatic glucose production
The HepG2 cells were seeded in 6 well culture plate at a con-
centration of 3 × 105 cells/well. After conﬂuence, cells were subjected
to treatment of DEX (500 nM) with or without PSTi8 (200, 500 nM) for
24 h and treated with insulin for last 20 min. Cells were washed with
PBS twice and 2 ml glucose production media added (without glucose
DMEM supplemented with 20 mM sodium lactate and 2 mM sodium
pyruvate). After 3–4 h incubation f– media was collected and lyophi-
lised for the measurement of glucose concentration by using Amplex
red glucose assay kit. The data was normalised by protein concentration
[24].
2.4. ATP/AMP ratio
For the analysis of ATP/AMP ratio, HepG2 cells were seeded at a
concentration of 8 × 105 cells/well in 60 mm culture dish. When cells
become conﬂuent, it was treated with DEX (500 nM), PSTi8 (200 nM)
for 24 h and insulin (100 nM) for last 20 min. Cells were then trypsi-
nised, washed with PBS and the resulting cell pellet was resuspended in
200 μl of ice-cold 5% w/v trichloroacetic acid (TCA). For liver tissue,
homogenized in same TCA for 5 min. After that it was vortexed and
centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 5 min to remove cell debris. The acid so-
luble fraction was neutralised by diethyl ether up to three extractions
and then lyophilised. For analysis of nucleotide, cells was passed
through 0.22 μm ﬁlter unit prior to injection in phenomenex Jupiter
C18 (250 × 4.6 mm, 4μ) proteo 90 Å; California, USA. Samples were
eluted at ﬂow rate of 0.4 ml/min by using methanol and phosphate
buﬀer 0.1 M in a ratio of 5:95 and absorbance was measured at 254 nm
by HPLC, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan. Nucleotide was detected by using
their absorbance and compared with the standard solution of ATP and
AMP. From the calibration standard, ratio of ATP and AMP present in
sample was estimated by normalising with the protein concentration
[25].
2.5. Oil red O staining
HepG2 cells were cultured at a concentration of 5 × 104 in 96-well
culture plate. After 80–90 % conﬂuence the media was changed and
treated with DEX with diﬀerent doses from (500, 1000, 1500 nM) with
or without PSTi8 (200, 500 nM) and kaempferol (2.5 μg/ml) for 24 h.
The media was removed, washed twice with PBS and stained with Oil
Red O. After washing and complete drying, isopropanol was added,
followed by 10 min incubation at room temperature. The solution was
transferred to another 96 well plate to measure absorbance at 540 nm
wavelength.

2.7. Animal model development and treatments
7-8 weeks old male C57BL/6 mice (20 ± 2 g) were obtained from
the Laboratory Animal Facility of CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute
(CDRI), Lucknow, India used in the present study. All procedures in-
volving mice were approved by the Institutional Animal Ethics
Committee of CSIR-CDRI (IAEC/2015/69) and were in accordance with
Committee for the purpose of control and supervision of experiments on
animals (CPCSEA guidelines). The animals were housed in poly-
propylene cages in the animal house, with temperature 25 ± 2 0C,
relative humidity 60–70%, light 300 Lx at ﬂoor level with regular 12 h
light cycle. The animals were given standard pellet diet and drinking
water ad libitum during the experimental period. We have divided 24
mice randomly into 4 groups: 1st vehicle control, 2nd DEX group, 3rd
treated (DEX + PSTi8 acute) and 4th treated (DEX + PSTi8 chronic)
group, (n = 6). Control group treated with saline. DEX and DEX+PSTi8
treated group received DEX for 17 days [26]. The chronic treatment
group received PSTi8 from 8th day of DEX treatment upto 17th day (10
days). The acute treated group received PSTi8 at 30 min before the
experiments. At last we have sacriﬁced the animals and collected tissue
samples and blood for further analyses.
2.8. Glucose, insulin and pyruvate tolerance test
Glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT), insulin tolerance test (IPITT) and
pyruvate tolerance test (IPPTT) were carried out in mice after 6 h of
fasting. The blood glucose levels were measured from tail tip using
Contour TS blood glucose meter. Mice were administered IP PSTi8
acute 5 mg/kg, chronic 2 mg/kg for 10 days and injected before 30 min
of glucose/insulin/pyruvate load. To determine the blood glucose le-
vels, after post-glucose, insulin and pyruvate load, blood samples were
taken at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120 min following IP injection of glucose
(1.5 g/kg), insulin (0.4 IU/kg) and pyruvate (1 g/kg) body weight. AUC
was calculated using standard [17].
2.9. Indirect calorimeter
Metabolic measurements in animals were obtained by using
Oxymax compressive animal lab animal monitoring system (Oxymax-
CLAMS) from Columbus instrument, Columbus, USA. Before starting
the experiment, system was calibrated with the standard gas mixture.
Animals were housed in a single cage chamber for the measurement of
oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide release, heat production, re-
spiratory exchange ratio (RER) and food, water intake. These mea-
surements were observed for three days. The 2nd day stable data was
used to measure the metabolic response of DEX with or without PSTi8.
Energy expenditure (heat) was calculated using the equation EE =
(3.815 + 1.232 x RER) x VO2 [27].
2.10. Body composition analysis
EchoMRI body composition analyzer (E26-226-RM EchoMRI LLC,
USA) was used for analysis of body composition of animals through
radio frequency pulses applied at distinct static magnetic ﬁeld. During
the measurement period, each mouse was placed into a thin wall plastic
cylinder (4.5 cm diameter), maintained at limited access for vertical
and horizontal movements [28].
2.11. Ex-vivo imaging
For the analysis of PSTi8 distribution ex-vivo imaging was per-
formed on an In-Vivo Imaging System (IVIS), PerkinElemer, Waltham,
USA. Sulphorhodamine b labelled PSTi8 were synthesized and puriﬁed
from Genpro Biotech, India. Mice were administered with ﬂuorescence
tagged PSTi8 (5 mg/kg) through IP route. After 30 min mice were sa-
criﬁced and excised organ were imaged with excitation 535 nm and
emission 580 nm. The data was represented as total ﬂux (photon/
second).
2.12. Measurement of glycogen, PKC activity and triglyceride level in liver
Glycogen content, protein kinase C (PKC) activity and triglyceride
(TG) levels were measured in liver tissue as per manufacturer’s protocol
mentioned in Glycogen Colorimetric/Fluorometric Assay Kit [29], PKC
kinase activity kit and Triglyceride calorimetric assay kit respectively.
2.13. Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
Production of ROS in liver tissue and HepG2 cells were measured
using H2DCFDA ﬂuorescence method. In brief, for ex-vivo sample liver
tissue was homogenized in Tris-buﬀer, centrifuged and supernatant was
collected. Incubated supernatant with H2DCFDA for 30 min in dark and
measured the ﬂuorescence at excitation 488 and emission 530 nm. The
total ROS production was analysed by normalization with protein
concentration [30]. For in-vitro ROS analysis, HepG2 cells were seeded
in 96 well plates and treated with DEX with or without PSTi8 (200,
500 nM) and kaempferol (2.5 μg/ml) for 24 h and measured by
H2DCFDA method as described previously [31].

2.19. Statistical method
Results were expressed as Mean ± SEM. All the data were analysed
using Prism software version 5.0 (GraphPad software, San Diego, CA,

3. Results
3.1. PSTi8 inhibits lipid deposition, hepatic glucose production and
stimulates cellular ATP and AMPK activity
Imbalance in glucose and lipid homeostasis caused by glucocorti-
coid was studied in DEX-induced HepG2 cells with or without PSTi8
treatment. In HepG2 cells, PSTi8 inhibits lipid droplet deposition more
signiﬁcantly at 200 nM (P < 0.01) as compare to 500 nM (P < 0.05)
with an increasing concentration of DEX (Fig. 1a). The increase in lipid
deposition on DEX treatment was also associated with oxidative stress
as seen by ROS production (Fig. 1b). Kaempferol was used as positive
control (fatty acid synthesis inhibitor). The increase in lipid deposition
and ROS production was further conﬁrmed by increase mRNA expres-
sion of lipogeneic Srebp-1c, Fas genes and inﬂammatory NF-κB and IL-6
genes which was signiﬁcantly decreased by PSTi8 treatment (Fig. 1c,
P < 0.05). Further we evaluated PSTi8 eﬀect on gluconeogenesis and
found that PSTi8 at 200 nM signiﬁcantly decrease hepatic glucose re-
lease (Fig. 1d, P < 0.05), supress the protein expression of gluconeo-
genic genes PEPCK (Fig. 1e, P < 0.05) and G6Pase (Fig. 1f, P < 0.01)
in DEX induced IR HepG2 cells. PSTi8 also enhance the cellular energy
(ATP/AMP) ratio (Fig. 1g, P < 0.05) in DEX induced IR HepG2 cells. In
HepG2 cells PSTi8 at 200 nM signiﬁcantly stimulates phosphorylation
of Thr 172 AMPKα in comparision to untreated cells (Fig. 1h,
P < 0.05). We have also analysed eﬀect of PSTi8 on insulin signalling
components IR-β and phosphorylation of Thr308 AKT in HepG2 cells
and found increse in IR-β expression (Supplementary Fig. S1) but no
change in p- Thr308 AKT (Supplementary Fig. S2).

4. Discussion
In recent study, we have showed that PSTi8 act as a PST inhibitor
[17]. In this study, we found that PSTi8 ameliorate fatty liver diseases
and improves glucose homeostasis through the activation of AMPK
signalling pathway by GRP78 in DEX-induced mice. Furthermore,
PSTi8 inhibits lipid deposition and stimulate lipid oxidation in liver, as
a result it enhances insulin sensitivity and supress oxidative stress.
These ﬁndings reveal one of the cellular mechanism by which PSTi8
reduce lipogenesis and enhance insulin sensitivity on GC challenge to
improve glucose and lipid homeostasis.
T2DM is a complex metabolic syndrome and develops due to in-
creased whole body IR through accumulation of lipid or by hypergly-
caemia [34–36]. DEX is one of the major GC which on binding with GC
receptor activate gluconeogenesis which enhances hepatic glucose
production and lead to hyperglycaemia. The enhanced hepatic glucose
production/hyperglycaemia attenuates AMPK activity and stimulates
lipogenesis and IR [14,15,37,38]. PSTi8 was found to be eﬀectively
regulating the DEX eﬀect on lipogenesis, IR and glucose metabolism. It
inhibits fat accumulation in both liver and cultured hepatocytes by

niﬁcantly enhances AMPK phosphorylation (Fig. 5a) in liver tissue. The
enhanced phosphorylation of AMPK was due to increased catalytic
ATPase activity of GRP78 (Fig. 5d) [18,19,40] which in turn inhibits
formation of mature Srebp-1c by increasing phosphorylation at Ser372
(Fig. 5b). But there was no change observed in Srebp-1c expression at
transcriptional level (Fig. 5e) which suggest that AMPK modulate
Srebp-1c at post translational level [41]. PSTi8 treatment regulates Acc
gene expression by decreasing mRNA expression (Fig. 5e) [42] and at
post-translation level by increasing its inhibitory phosphorylation
(Fig. 5c) through activated AMPK pathway [21]. Decreased formation
of mature Srebp-1c and inactivation or suppression of Acc leads to
decreased gene expression of Ppar-γ (Fig. 5e). This reduces lipid de-
position [43] as shown by decreased LDL level (Fig. 3j), hepatic TG
(Fig. 3i), lipid droplet in hepatocytes (Fig. 1a), fat mass (Fig. 2h) and
increased HDL plasma circulating level (Fig. 3k). The oxidation of fat
and its clearance is always required to maintain lipid homeostasis. In
DEX induced mice, oxidation of fat did not cope with on-going synthesis
due to increased plasma leptin (Fig. 2g) and decreased adiponectin
(insulin sensitizing adipokine) (Fig. 3h) which imbalance energy
homeostasis [44,45]. So, the increased synthesis of fat in liver act as
source of lipid-peroxide which is responsible for ROS generated stress.
The progression of oxidative stress by lipid-peroxide result in in-
ﬂammation and activation of NF-κB signalling that causes development
of steatosis which leads to IR [46]. Administration of PSTi8 enhances
energy expenditure through lipid oxidation by increasing UCP3 (Fig. 5f)
[47], adiponectin (Fig. 3h) Cpt-1a, PGC-1α, ACOX1 (Fig. 5e) expression
and clear extra hepatic fat deposition caused by DEX [48] as well as
suppresses the oxidative ROS production (Fig. 3l). The decrease in ROS
production occurs due to complete oxidation of lipid and/or less lipid
peroxide formation which lead to inhibition of NF-κB (Fig. 5h) signal-
ling pathway and reduced pro-inﬂammatory cytokines TNF-α expres-
sion (Fig. 5i). Furthermore the increase in fatty acid oxidation was also
coupled with increased ATP/AMP ratio both in-vitro and in-vivo
(Figs. 1g, 5 g) [49].
The increase in lipid oxidation also altered the physiological para-
meters such as RER, heat, VO2 and VCO2. RER value indicates which
fuel (carbohydrate or fat) is being metabolised to supply energy in the
body. DEX causes insigniﬁcant decrease in RER which indicate trigger
in fat oxidation but couldn’t maintain the balance between synthesis
and oxidation whereas treatment of PSTi8 trigger fat oxidation by de-
creasing RER value [50] signiﬁcantly (Fig. 4e and f).The lipid oxidation
was also accomplished with increase in O2 consumption [50] and CO2
evolution [51] on PSTi8 treatment (Fig. 4c, d, a and b). Energy pro-
duction (heat) responsible for thermoregulation is directly correlated
with fatty acid oxidation [52]. Administration of DEX increases heat
production insigniﬁcantly in DC (indicating increased fatty acid
synthesis and decreased oxidation) and signiﬁcantly LC (decreased
synthesise and increased oxidation), this paradox can be explained by
more food consumption on DEX treatment (Fig. 4j) increases hepatic
de-novo fatty acid synthesis. While treatment of PSTi8 did not decreses
food intake but signiﬁcantly increases energy expenditure in both the
cycle (Fig. 4g and h) by increasing fat oxidation and maintain lipid
homeostasis in DEX-induced mice.
DEX not only impairs lipid metabolism but also causes IR. As
mentioned previously, besides Acc role in lipogenesis, Acc also en-
hances PKC activity by translocating it from cytosol to plasma mem-
brane [51]. The increase in kinases activity of PKC leads to the phos-
phorylation of IRS-1 at Ser612 [53] which reduces insulin stimulated
AKT activity. As mentioned in (Fig. 5e and c) that PSTi8 downregulate
Acc expression and increased inhibitory phosphorylation of Ser79Acc
which inhibits PKC kinases activity (Fig. 3d). The decrease in enzymatic
activity of PKC increases insulin sensitivity and glucose clearance
(Fig. 2a, b and e, f) respectively as shown by decreased Ser612 phos-
phorylation of IRS-1 (Fig. 6a) and increased phosphorylation of
Thr308AKT (Fig. 6c). In addition, it causes increased Ser256FoxO1
phosphorylation (Fig. 6d) and suppression of gluconeogenic genes,
proteins expression of G6Pase, PEPCK, FBPase (Figs. 1e, f and 6 g-i)
which inhibits hepatic glucose production both in-vitro and in-vivo
(Figs. 1d, 2 c and 2 d). In context to decreased hepatic glucose pro-
duction we have also found lower plasma glucagon level on PSTi8
treatment (Fig. 3f). Activation of AKT also stimulates phosphorylation
of Ser9GSK3β (Fig. 6e) responsible for glycogen synthesis [54] and
suppress GP mRNA expression [55] (Fig. 6f) which causes increased
glycogenesis (Fig. 3e) and decreased glycogenolysis in liver. The re-
duced insulin sensitivity in presences of DEX also causes development
of hyperinsulimia (Fig. 3b), increased HOMA-IR (Fig. 3a), higher
plasma PST level (chromogranin A derived peptide) (Fig. 3c) and
downregulation of IRβ expression (Fig. 6b) which further stimulates
insulin resistance. Furthermore we revealed that these eﬀects of DEX
were attenuated by PSTi8 administration and enhance insulin sensi-
tivity in DEX-induced mice. The change in physiological parameters on
PSTi8 treatment and the possible mechanism of action is represented in
(Fig. 7).
5. Conclusion
Our study elucidated that PSTi8 treatment reduces fatty acid
synthesis, increase its oxidation to enhance insulin sensitivity and
maintain glucose and lipid homeostasis in DEX-induced fatty liver
disease associated diabetic mice. The data from present study suggest
that activation of AMPK by PSTi8 through GRP78 inhibit lipogenesis
and enhance fatty acid oxidation through upregulation of UCP3, to
supress oxidative stress. The Activated AMPK also enhances insulin
sensitivity through the inhibition of PKC kinase activity. Thus PSTi8
improved glucose and lipid metabolism to combat the risk of fatty liver
disease associated T2DM.
